title: Reading Financial Statements
intro: A company's accounts tell you what it earns, what it owns and owes, and where its cash really goes. You don't need to be an accountant to read them; you need to know the three statements, how they connect, and the handful of ratios that answer most questions.

blocks.text: US public companies file a yearly report (the 10-K) and quarterly reports (10-Q) with the Securities and Exchange Commission; all are free on the SEC's EDGAR website. Companies elsewhere publish annual reports under IFRS (International Financial Reporting Standards) rules; US companies use US GAAP (Generally Accepted Accounting Principles). The two are broadly similar. Read the notes and the management discussion (MD&A), not only the tables: the notes are where the accounting choices and the risks are explained.
The income statement (profit and loss, P&L) covers a period, usually a quarter or a year. It runs from sales at the top to profit at the bottom:

blocks.source:
Revenue (sales)                         1,000
- Cost of goods sold (COGS)               -600
= Gross profit                             400     gross margin 40%
- Operating expenses (SG&A, R&D)           -220
- Depreciation and amortization             -50
= Operating income (EBIT)                  130     operating margin 13%
- Interest expense                          -20
= Pre-tax income                           110
- Income tax (21%)                          -23
= Net income                                87     net margin 8.7%

Shares outstanding 50  ->  earnings per share (EPS) = 87 / 50 = 1.74

items: EBIT (earnings before interest and taxes) measures the business's operating profit regardless of how it is financed. EBITDA adds back depreciation and amortization; it is popular because it ignores the cost of replacing equipment, which is also why Warren Buffett and others distrust it.
Diluted EPS counts shares that options and convertible bonds could create.

Adjusted or non-GAAP earnings strip out items management calls one-off. Check whether the same 'one-off' charges come back every year, and whether stock-based compensation has been excluded: it is a real cost to shareholders.

blocks.text: The balance sheet is a snapshot on one date of what the company owns (assets) and how they were paid for: by borrowing (liabilities) or by owners (shareholders' equity). It always balances:

items: Current assets turn into cash within a year: cash, receivables (money customers owe), inventory. Current liabilities are due within a year: payables, short-term debt.

Long-term assets: property, plant and equipment (PP&E) at cost less accumulated depreciation; intangible assets; goodwill, the premium paid for acquisitions over the target's book value, which is written down if the deal sours.

Equity (book value) is what would be left for owners if assets were sold at their book values and every debt paid. Market value is usually far above book value for companies whose main assets (brands, software, people) are not on the balance sheet at all.

blocks.text: Profit is an opinion; cash is a fact. Accrual accounting records revenue when it is earned and costs when they are incurred, which can differ a lot from when cash moves. The cash flow statement starts from net income and reconciles to the actual change in cash, in three parts:

items: Operating cash flow (CFO): net income plus non-cash charges (depreciation, stock pay) plus or minus changes in working capital (receivables, inventory, payables).
Investing cash flow: capital expenditures (capex), acquisitions, purchases and sales of investments.
Financing cash flow: borrowing and repaying debt, issuing and buying back shares, paying dividends.

blocks.text: Free cash flow (FCF) is the cash the business produces after keeping itself going and growing: $FCF = CFO - \text{capex}$. It is the quantity a discounted cash flow valuation discounts. A company whose net income runs far ahead of its operating cash flow year after year deserves a closer look: receivables may be piling up, or revenue booked too early.

blocks.alt: Diagram linking the three financial statements: net income from the income statement starts the cash flow statement and adds to retained earnings in the balance sheet's equity; the cash flow statement's ending cash becomes the cash line at the top of the balance sheet.
blocks.caption: How the three statements connect: profit flows into equity, and the cash flow statement explains the change in the balance sheet's cash.

items: Margins: gross, operating and net profit as a share of revenue. Compare with the company's own history and its competitors, not across industries (a supermarket's 3% net margin is healthy; a software company's would not be).
Return on equity: $ROE = \text{net income} / \text{equity}$. How much profit the owners' money produces. Debt raises ROE, so look at it beside leverage.

Return on invested capital: $ROIC = \text{EBIT}(1 - t) / (\text{debt} + \text{equity} - \text{cash})$. How much the whole business earns on all the capital in it. A company that earns more than its cost of capital (often 7 to 10%) creates value when it grows; one that earns less destroys value by growing.

blocks.text: The DuPont identity splits ROE into three levers, telling you whether a high ROE comes from fat margins, efficient use of assets, or borrowing:

items: Debt to equity and net debt to EBITDA (debt minus cash, over EBITDA). Below about 2 is comfortable for most industries; above 4 is heavy.
Interest coverage: EBIT / interest expense. Below about 3 means a bad year could make interest hard to pay.
Current ratio: current assets / current liabilities, a rough test of short-term liquidity.
Asset turnover: sales / assets.
Days sales outstanding: receivables / revenue $\times$ 365. A rise may mean customers are paying slowly or sales are being pulled forward.
Inventory days and payable days; the cash conversion cycle is inventory days plus receivable days minus payable days.

Accruals: net income minus operating cash flow, scaled by assets. Research by Richard Sloan (1996) found that companies with high accruals (earnings not backed by cash) went on to earn lower stock returns.
Earnings rising while operating cash flow falls.
Receivables or inventory growing much faster than sales.
Frequent 'one-off' restructuring charges, changes of auditor, late filings, or changes to how revenue is recognized.
Goodwill a large share of assets after a string of acquisitions.
Heavy insider selling, or management pay tied to adjusted metrics they define themselves.

blocks.title: DuPont
blocks.text: Company A has a net margin of 5%, asset turnover of 2.0 and assets / equity of 3.0. Company B has a net margin of 20%, turnover of 0.5 and assets / equity of 1.5. Compute each ROE and say where it comes from.
solution: A: $0.05 \times 2.0 \times 3.0 = 30\%$, from fast turnover and heavy leverage (a retailer, say).
B: $0.20 \times 0.5 \times 1.5 = 15\%$, from fat margins with little debt (perhaps a software or brand business). A's higher ROE comes with much more financial risk.

blocks.title: Free cash flow
blocks.text: A company reports net income of \$200 million, depreciation of \$80 million, stock-based compensation of \$30 million, an increase in receivables of \$60 million and capital expenditure of \$120 million. Estimate its operating cash flow and free cash flow.
solution: $CFO \approx 200 + 80 + 30 - 60 = \$250$ million (the receivables increase is profit not yet received in cash).
$FCF = 250 - 120 = \$130$ million. Some analysts also subtract the \$30 million of stock pay, since it costs owners through dilution, giving \$100 million.
blocks.answer: CFO about \$250 m; FCF about \$130 m

blocks.title: Coverage
blocks.text: A company has EBIT of \$45 million and \$600 million of debt at 6% interest. What is its interest coverage, and how far can EBIT fall before coverage drops to 1.5?
solution: Interest $= 0.06 \times 600 = \$36$ million; coverage $= 45 / 36 = 1.25$. It is already below 1.5.
This company is fragile: a modest fall in profit would leave it unable to pay interest from operations.
